prompt: Which of these changes what an on-demand query is billed?
hint: Three things fix the bill before the query runs.

choices.text: A filter `store_id = 7` on a table partitioned by `dt` only
choices.why: A filter on another column reads the column; it prunes nothing.

choices.text: Adding `LIMIT 100`
choices.why: The rows returned do not change the bytes read.

choices.text: Naming one column fewer
choices.why: Right. Every column referenced is billed.

choices.text: Asking for the result in JSON
choices.why: The output format has nothing to do with the bytes read.

prompt: A query references `dt` only in its `WHERE`, and reads 594,882 rows of a partitioned table. How many bytes does `dt` add to what it processes?
hint: A `DATE` is 8 bytes.

prompt: `bqbill.py` printed 15,023,069 bytes processed and 15,728,640 billed. What makes the difference?
hint: Divide the billed number by 1,048,576.

choices.text: The 10 MB minimum
choices.why: 15 MB is already above the minimum.

choices.text: The rounding up to the next MB
choices.why: Right. 15,728,640 is exactly 15 MB.

choices.text: Compression of the Parquet files
choices.why: Compression lowers bytes on disk, never the billed ones.

choices.text: The bytes of the files' footers
choices.why: Footers are not in the logical size at all.

prompt: Why does `bqbill.py` accept a range of `dt` and no other filter?
hint: Which filter changes which rows are counted?

choices.text: DuckDB cannot filter on other columns
choices.why: DuckDB filters on anything; the program refuses on purpose.

choices.text: Only the partition filter changes the bytes billed
choices.why: Right. Any other filter is billed for its column and prunes nothing.

choices.text: Filters on strings are billed twice
choices.why: No column is billed twice; it is counted once if referenced.

choices.text: Other filters make the bill depend on the cache
choices.why: The cache depends on the whole query and the tables, not on its filters.

prompt: What does a dry run cost on BigQuery?
hint: The query is planned, not run.

choices.text: The 10 MB minimum
choices.why: The minimum applies to queries that run.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. It reports the bytes and reads none.

choices.text: The bytes of the table's metadata
choices.why: Metadata is not billed as query bytes.

choices.text: Half of the estimate it prints
choices.why: There is no partial charge for an estimate.

prompt: A query has `maximum_bytes_billed` set to 1 GiB and would be billed 3 GiB. What happens?
hint: The limit acts before anything is read.

choices.text: It runs and is billed 1 GiB
choices.why: There is no capped bill; the query either runs in full or not at all.

choices.text: It reads the first GiB and stops
choices.why: Nothing is read: it fails before starting.

choices.text: It fails with an error and costs nothing
choices.why: Right. That is the per-query guardrail.

choices.text: It moves to a reservation to finish
choices.why: No limit changes a query's pricing model.

prompt: The nightly transformation bills 400 GiB, and somebody sets `maximum_bytes_billed` to 1 GiB on every query of the project's code. What does this lesson predict?
hint: The limit is chosen per query.

choices.text: A safer night
choices.why: The night's job is refused every time it runs.

choices.text: The transformation is refused every night
choices.why: Right. A limit fitted to the dashboard is wrong for the large job.

choices.text: The transformation runs, billed at 1 GiB
choices.why: There is no capped bill; it fails.

choices.text: Nothing, since the limit only applies to dashboards
choices.why: It applies to whatever query carries it.

prompt: The `bq` flag that asks BigQuery for the bytes a query would process, without running it, is `--___`.
hint: Two words joined by an underscore.

prompt: In which direction is a DuckDB plan read?
hint: Where is the table read?

choices.text: From the bottom up
choices.why: Right. Each step hands rows to the one above it.

choices.text: From the top, in the order the SQL is written
choices.why: SQL's order is not the order of execution.

choices.text: Left to right, one column per step
choices.why: The boxes are stacked by step, not by column.

choices.text: In any order, since all steps run at once
choices.why: Each step depends on the rows of the one below.

prompt: The plan of the district query lists only `district` and `total_cents` as projections. Why is `dt` missing?
hint: Where does `dt` live in these files?

choices.text: The filter on `dt` was dropped
choices.why: It is right there under File Filters.

choices.text: `dt` is too small to list
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with the projections.

choices.text: It came from the folder names
choices.why: Right. In BigQuery `dt` is a column and is billed.

choices.text: Only `SELECT`ed columns are ever projected
choices.why: Filter columns are read too when they are columns.

prompt: `HASH_GROUP_BY` received 594,882 rows and produced 8. How many rows went in for each one that came out? Round to a whole number.
hint: Divide.

prompt: A query meant for one day shows `Scanning Files: 60/60` in its plan. What has the plan caught?
hint: The file count is the partitions read.

choices.text: A filter that did not prune
choices.why: Right. That is the expensive mistake, caught in advance.

choices.text: A slow laptop
choices.why: The count is about files, not speed.

choices.text: Too many slots
choices.why: DuckDB has no slots.

choices.text: A day with too many orders for one file
choices.why: One day would be one file however many orders it had.

prompt: In a stage, the maximum compute time is ten times the average. What does the documentation call this, and what usually causes it?
hint: The stage ends when its slowest worker does.

choices.text: Slot contention, from other queries
choices.why: Contention shows as waiting, not as one worker computing longer.

choices.text: Skew: one key value far more common than the rest
choices.why: Right. One worker was given far more than the others.

choices.text: A cache miss
choices.why: The cache answers whole queries, not stages.

choices.text: Insufficient shuffle quota
choices.why: That shows as shuffle bytes spilled to disk.

prompt: A job used 120,000 slot-milliseconds and took 4 seconds. How many slots did it hold on average?
hint: Slot time divided by elapsed time, in the same unit.

prompt: Why do the first stage's workers already sum `total_cents` per district before the shuffle?
hint: Compare what would cross the network either way.

choices.text: BigQuery bills fewer bytes for partial sums
choices.why: On demand, the bill was fixed before the graph existed.

choices.text: So that a few rows per worker cross the shuffle instead of every order
choices.why: Right. That is where the query becomes cheap to move.

choices.text: Because the second stage cannot add
choices.why: It finishes the aggregation from the partials.

choices.text: To sort the answer earlier
choices.why: The sort is the last stage's.

prompt: Which bytes does BigQuery bill on demand?
hint: A price list has to be knowable in advance.

choices.text: The compressed bytes its engine reads
choices.why: Those depend on compression and are never what is billed.

choices.text: The logical bytes, by type
choices.why: Right. Uncompressed, value by value.

choices.text: The bytes of the result
choices.why: The result size does not enter the bill.

choices.text: The physical bytes of the whole table
choices.why: Only referenced columns count, and logically.

prompt: `district` is 230,035 bytes on disk for September and about 5.5 million on the bill. Why so far apart?
hint: Eight values, nearly 600,000 rows.

choices.text: BigQuery stores strings uncompressed, unlike Parquet
choices.why: It compresses them; it bills them as if it did not.

choices.text: Parquet stores each name once, in a dictionary
choices.why: Right. `RLE_DICTIONARY` in the encodings.

choices.text: Accented names count double
choices.why: Accents add one byte each in UTF-8, nowhere near the gap.

choices.text: The bill includes `dt`
choices.why: `dt` is its own 4,759,056; this is `district` alone.

prompt: A notebook pulls `orders` out of BigQuery through the Storage Read API. What does it pay for, by the pricing page?
hint: Same rule, another price.

choices.text: Logical bytes, at 1.98 USD per TiB past 300 free
choices.why: Right. The size by type, again.

choices.text: The compressed bytes sent over the network to the notebook
choices.why: The page bills by data type size, not by what crosses the wire.

choices.text: Nothing, since it is not a query
choices.why: It has its own price on the page.

choices.text: 11.25 USD per TiB, as a query
choices.why: That is on demand; the Storage Read API has its own line.

prompt: Put the three stages of the district query in the order BigQuery runs them.
hint: Partials come before totals.
items: Read September's two columns and sum per district for each worker's share
Shuffle by district and finish the sums
Sort the eight totals and write the answer

hint: One right-hand question has no tool here.

prompt: Which of these were measured in this lesson rather than computed or taken from Google's documentation? Choose all that apply.
hint: DuckDB and the Parquet footers measured; the rest was computed or documented.

choices.text: September's two columns occupy 2,978,159 bytes on disk
choices.why: Yes, from `parquet_metadata`.

choices.text: `HASH_GROUP_BY` turned 594,882 rows into 8
choices.why: Yes, from `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.

choices.text: The district query would be billed 15,728,640 bytes
choices.why: Computed by `bqbill.py` from documented sizes.

choices.text: BigQuery runs it in three stages
choices.why: An illustration after the documentation; no job ran.
